title: Weak stability tested on the first Frobenius root field
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field] of positive characteristic $p$, with a nontrivial real-valued multiplicative nonarchimedean absolute value $|\cdot|$. In an algebraic closure $\overline K$, put $K_1=\{z\in\overline K:z^p\in K\}$ and $N(z)=|z^p|^{1/p}$. Assume that for every finite-dimensional $K$-linear subspace $V\subseteq K_1$ and every basis $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ of $V$ there are real $c_V,C_V>0$ such that $$c_V\max_i|a_i|\le N(\sum_i a_iv_i)\le C_V\max_i|a_i|\qquad(a_i\in K).$$ For $V=0$, the empty sum and maximum are zero. Then, for every finite field extension $L/K$ and every basis $w_1,\ldots,w_d$ of $L$, its minimal-polynomial spectral norm $s_{L/K}$ [lem-trf-incomplete-spectral-algebra-norm] satisfies $$c\max_i|b_i|\le s_{L/K}(\sum_i b_iw_i)\le C\max_i|b_i|\qquad(b_i\in K)$$ for some real $c,C>0$. No completeness of $K$, finiteness of $K_1/K$, or separability of $L/K$ is assumed.

proof.text: The characteristic $p$ of a field is prime. The identities $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$ and $(xy)^p=x^py^p$ show that $K_1$ is a field containing $K$, and that $N$ is a definite multiplicative ultrametric absolute value extending $|\cdot|$: for example $N(x+y)^p\le\max(N(x)^p,N(y)^p)$ and $N(ax)^p=|a|^pN(x)^p$. Its restriction to $K$ is nontrivial. Apply [lem-sfb-normed-field-completion] to $K$ and $(K_1,N)$, obtaining complete normed fields $H=\widehat K$ and $H_1=\widehat {K_1}$. The isometry $K\to K_1$ extends to an isometric field embedding $H\to H_1$: send a Cauchy sequence in $K$ to the same sequence in $K_1$. Equal classes have differences tending to zero; conversely an image of norm zero has original norm zero. Sums and products of representatives give the field-map identities. The ultrametric inequalities pass to limits in both completions.

proof.text: Use [def-weil-vector-space-scalar-extension] to form the commutative algebra $B=K_1\otimes_K H$, and define $j:B\to H_1$ by $z\otimes h\mapsto zh$, with the embeddings from step 1. This is a well-defined algebra map by bilinearity and the displayed tensor multiplication. Every $u\in B$ is a finite sum of pure tensors. Choose a $K$-basis $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ of the span of their first factors and rewrite $u=\sum_i v_i\otimes h_i$. Choose sequences $a_{i,m}\in K$ converging to $h_i$, possible by the definition of $H$. The assumed lower bound for this particular finite-dimensional span gives $$N(\sum_i a_{i,m}v_i)\ge c_V\max_i|a_{i,m}|.$$ Finite sums and the absolute value are continuous, so passage to the limit in $H_1$ gives $$|j(u)|_{H_1}\ge c_V\max_i|h_i|_H.$$ Thus $j(u)=0$ forces all $h_i=0$ and hence $u=0$. This includes the empty span. Since a field has no nonzero nilpotents, injectivity of $j$ shows that $B$ is reduced: $u^m=0$ implies $j(u)^m=0$, then $j(u)=0$, then $u=0$.

proof.text: Interchange tensor factors to identify $H\otimes_K K_1$ with $B$, by $h\otimes z\mapsto z\otimes h$. It is reduced by step 2. Apply [lem-trf-first-root-tensor-reduced-test] with $k=K$, $F=H$, and $E=L$. Its first-root field is exactly the given $K_1$, the prime characteristic hypothesis holds, and it requires no algebraicity of $H/K$. Therefore $A=L\otimes_K H$ is reduced, after interchanging factors once more. This argument applies to every finite $L/K$, including purely inseparable extensions.

Fix any given basis $w_1,\ldots,w_d$ of $L/K$. By [def-weil-vector-space-scalar-extension], $w_i\otimes1$ form an $H$-basis of $A$, so $\dim_H A=d\ge1$ and the map $L\to A$, $z\mapsto z\otimes1$, is injective. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dim-algebra-artinian], $A$ is Artinian. Its reducedness from step 3 lets us apply [lem-sfb-reduced-artinian-residue-product], obtaining the canonical product of residue fields $A\simeq\prod_{j=1}^r E_j$. Here $r\ge1$, since $A\ne0$; each quotient $E_j$ is spanned over $H$ by the images of the $d$ basis vectors, hence is finite-dimensional over $H$. The structural map $H\to E_j$ is a unital field map and therefore injective; the product isomorphism is an $H$-algebra isomorphism because each coordinate is the quotient map.

proof.text: For each finite field extension $E_j/H$, [lem-trf-spectral-norm-algebraic-extension] supplies its multiplicative ultrametric spectral norm $s_j$, since $H$ is complete and nontrivially valued. Put $Q(a)=\max_j s_j(a_j)$ on the product, and transport it to $A$. This is definite, ultrametric, scalar homogeneous, submultiplicative, satisfies $Q(1)=1$, and $Q(a^m)=Q(a)^m$ for $m\ge1$, by the same identities in each component and the nonempty finite maximum. In particular $A$ is a finite-dimensional Hausdorff topological $H$-vector space: the norm inequalities give continuity of addition, and $$Q(ha-h_0a_0)\le\max(|h|Q(a-a_0),|h-h_0|Q(a_0))$$ gives continuity of scalar multiplication.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-finite-dimensional-linear-map-continuous] to the $H$-linear coordinate maps for the basis $w_i\otimes1$ of $(A,Q)$. The base $H$ is complete with a nontrivial absolute value, the source is finite-dimensional and Hausdorff by steps 4–5, and the target $H$ is a topological vector space. Thus there is $\delta>0$ such that $Q(a)<\delta$ implies $\max_i|a_i|<1$. Choose $t\in H$ with $0<\rho=|t|<1$, replacing a nontrivially valued element by its inverse if necessary. For $a\ne0$, choose $m\in\mathbf Z$ so that $\rho\delta\le\rho^mQ(a)<\delta$. Applying the preceding implication to $t^ma$ gives $\max_i|a_i|<\rho^{-m}\le Q(a)/(\rho\delta)$. The case $a=0$ is immediate. Consequently $$c\max_i|a_i|\le Q(\sum_i a_i(w_i\otimes1))\le C\max_i|a_i|$$ with $c=\rho\delta>0$ and $C=\max_i Q(w_i\otimes1)>0$; the upper bound is the finite ultrametric triangle inequality.

proof.text: Restrict $Q$ to $L\hookrightarrow A$ and write $M(z)=Q(z\otimes1)$. By step 5 and injectivity in step 4, $M$ is a definite, normalized, power-multiplicative ultrametric $K$-algebra norm. Step 6 restricted to coefficients in $K$ gives its two-sided bounds for the originally specified basis $w_i$. All hypotheses of [lem-trf-product-topology-spectral-uniqueness] therefore hold with $N=M$, without any completeness assumption on $K$ or separability assumption on $L/K$. It gives $M=s_{L/K}$. Substitution in those same bounds proves exactly the claimed inequalities for this arbitrary finite extension and this arbitrary basis.
